chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
title: What Duke Ellington was to Jackson: psychologist and diplomat
summary: Jackson calls Ellington a great psychologist who wrote parts knowing how each man would play them.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Butter, I'd just like to ask you this. There have been -- I see that Duke Ellington's band, like Benny Goodman's band, has had so many alumni, so many guys that come in, in and out of the band, and it's like a stamp of approval; if anyone has ever spent one hour in one of those bands, he's considered an all-time great because of these great leaders if they just accepted you for a week or two weeks.
I'd just like to, for the record's sake, ask you confidentially, what was Duke like to you and how do you feel about him and how did you feel about him? How do you feel about him?
Well, I feel about Duke Ellington -- Duke Ellington to me was one of the most amazing men that I have ever known in life. He was a great psychologist. He was a great diplomat.
How do you mean a psychologist?

He could -- anyway that you want -- he wanted you to play you would play that way without you thinking about it, because he knew his men to the extent that when he would make an arrangement, he would give certain guys certain parts or certain solos that he knew how they was going to treat it before that they even started to play it, because he used to hear before he would put it down.
He knew what it was going to sound like.
